key_specs.lee_vhs_dispense_volume: Catalogue: 'as low as 10 nL up to milliliters' (MINSTAC outlet with nozzle: 10 nL to mL). Kit document: kit covers '500 microliters down to 20 nanoliters'. Handbook: 'Stated minimum dispense volumes may not be achievable in all cases'.
key_specs.lee_vhs_viscosity_statement: Kit document section 3: 'Using significantly viscous fluids above 30 centipoises will have difficulty being dispensed.' No numeric limit on the product pages.
key_specs.lee_vhs_low_pressure_warning: Kit document section 4: at lower pressure 'the droplet will have a reduced velocity ... Fluid will begin to collect at the tip and dispense volumes will become very erratic.' Starting pressure for water-like fluids 2-5 psig.
key_specs.lee_vhs_response: Response as low as 250 us, up to 1 kHz; minimum spike 0.35 ms (EPDM) or 0.5 ms (FKM/FFKM); do not exceed 500 mW average coil power; coil max 66 C
key_specs.lee_vhs_wetted_materials: PEEK, stainless steel, PPS, seal material (EPDM / FKM / FFKM), epoxy; nozzle: stainless, epoxy (not on PTFE-coated), synthetic sapphire
key_specs.lee_nozzles_062_minstac_8.9mm: INZA4650935K 0.005 in (0.13 mm) 35,000 Lohm; INZA4670915K 0.0075 in (0.19 mm) 15,400 Lohm; INZA6670915K same, PTFE-coated; INZA4710975H 0.010 in (0.25 mm) 7,500 Lohm
key_specs.lee_driver: IECX0501350A spike-and-hold driver, spike adjustable 0.1-5 ms, needs 24 V (20 W) spike supply, 3.2 V (2 W) hold supply and a 5 V TTL signal; screw terminals 1-6
key_specs.valve_connector: Two contact pins 0.025 in (0.64 mm) square on 0.100 in (2.54 mm) centres, bent 90 degrees to the body; mating lead assembly IHWX0248120A (24 in, 24 AWG PTFE, flying leads)
key_specs.valve_body_colour: Not stated on any page fetched
key_specs.my_sizing_estimate_not_sourced: 14 nL through the 0.19 mm orifice at 1.25 m/s is a 0.5 mm long slug delivered in about 0.4 ms, i.e. right at the valve's minimum spike time; with the 0.25 mm orifice it would need 0.23 ms (too short), with 0.13 mm about 0.9 ms but a slender jet. Orifice viscous drop at 30 mPa.s is of order 0.1 bar; feed-line inertia dominates, so the reservoir must sit within a few cm of the valve.
key_specs.option_b_DOD_marking_valves: Large-character 'DOD' coder valves are sold on AliExpress only as spare parts for specific printheads (seen on fetched results pages: 61.59 USD for a solenoid valve listed for the Willett 3150SI DOD printer; 30-205 USD for Citronix/Videojet/Domino valves, which are continuous-inkjet parts). No listing or data sheet I found gives nozzle diameter, drop volume or a viscosity range. Not recommended: undocumented, built for thin solvent inks and millimetre-size dots (the last clause is general knowledge, not from a fetched page).
key_specs.option_c_piezo: MicroFab MJ-AB/MJ-AT: orifices 20-80 um (MJ-ABL 80-120 um), fluid viscosity '< 20 cPs', surface tension 20-70 dynes/cm, quote-only (manufacturer page fetched) - fails both the 0.3 mm size and 30 mPa.s. Nordson PICO Pulse: quote-only, page blocked; search snippet says deposits from 0.5 nL, orifices 50-600 um. Chinese piezo jet valves: 821.79 and 986.69 USD on a fetched AliExpress results page (valve only, specs not readable); one Chinese SFJ2500 valve quoted at 4550 USD in a snippet. All exceed or consume the whole 1000 USD budget.
key_specs.option_d_DIY_published: Harris, Liu, Bush 2015 (full text read): droplets 0.5-1.4 mm from eight nozzles 0.50-1.40 mm, tested only with 20.9 cSt silicone oil (950 kg/m3, 20.6 mN/m, i.e. about 20 mPa.s), 0.16 < Oh < 0.28, 5 Hz, diameter repeatable to +/-0.5 % in a run and about +/-1 % day to day; nozzle points down, reservoir head sets the meniscus; ejection speed is not reported. Ionkin and Harris 2018 (abstract only): water and water-glycerol, 0.65-1.32 mm, variability under 1 %; viscosities not confirmed. DropGen V3 (OSHWA page): 'more than 1 mm down to less than 0.2 mm' with brass 3D-printer nozzles; no viscosity or speed data on the pages read. So 0.3 mm is inside the V3 claim but outside both papers' demonstrated range; 30 mPa.s is above the only oil viscosity demonstrated (about 20 mPa.s); upward firing at 1.0-1.5 m/s and 1 % speed repeatability are not demonstrated anywhere.

dims_mm.valve_drawing_callouts_MM_config: 0.83 in (21.2), 0.52 in (13.2), 0.22 in (5.6) boss, pin pitch 2.5; drawing not to scale - overall length about 34-40 by my reading, request the inspection drawing

note: Recommendation for a hobbyist: buy the Lee VHS evaluation kit (or the FFKM valve plus the PTFE-coated 0.0075 in nozzle) by quote and build a DropGen-style piezo generator in parallel as the cheap fallback. Unproven for this use: (1) 14 nL sits at Lee's stated floor (10-20 nL) while 30 mPa.s sits at Lee's stated 'difficulty' threshold, both at once; (2) the low launch speed wanted (1.0-1.5 m/s) is the low-pressure regime where Lee warns of fluid collecting at the tip and erratic volumes; (3) firing upward makes tip flooding worse; (4) no source gives shot-to-shot speed repeatability, so 1 % is an assumption; (5) EPDM (kit valve) and the wetted epoxy against acrylate monomers are untested - Lee offers material samples for compatibility tests; (6) stray 405 nm light can cure resin in the nozzle; (7) price is unknown until quoted and may take a third or more of the 1000 USD budget. The DIY piezo generator meets the budget but its body is about 50 mm wide at the nozzle (35 mm piezo disc), it is only demonstrated firing downward at low, unreported speed, and 0.3 mm with a 30 mPa.s liquid is outside its published data.

key_specs.my_estimate_not_sourced: At 28-30 C the Anycubic resin should be roughly 60-75 mPa.s (acrylates lose a few percent of viscosity per kelvin). Log mixing rule: 80 mPa.s resin plus 30-40 wt% of an 8 mPa.s monomer gives about 40-32 mPa.s.

note: No consumer 405 nm MSLA resin with a data-sheet viscosity at or below 60 mPa.s at 25-30 C was found. The best documented one is 75-85 mPa.s at 25 C; Elegoo's 'as low as 60' is unitless and the product was sold out. Nothing hobby-priced states surface tension, Ec or Dp. Options: design for 60-85 mPa.s, warm the nozzle and resin to about 40 C, dilute with monomer (item 2b), or use a clear LED-UV inkjet varnish and measure it yourself. Pigmented inkjet inks cure only tens of micrometres deep, so a clear grade matters for 0.3 mm droplets (general knowledge).

key_specs.comparison_basis: Apart from the quoted page statements, this comparison is general materials knowledge, not sourced from fetched pages
key_specs.PLA: Stiffest of the unfilled options and the most accurate to print, but softens near 55-60 C and creeps under sustained load even at 35 C; fair against isopropanol, poor against prolonged monomer contact. About 20-30 USD per kg (not verified).
key_specs.PETG: Softens near 80 C, low creep at 35 C, good against isopropanol and brief acrylate contact, prints large parts with little warping. Reasonable 405 nm tolerance in black.
key_specs.ASA: Softens near 100 C and is the most UV-stable, but styrenic plastics are attacked by ester monomers and can stress-crack with isopropanol; warps on large prints (Prusa says so).
key_specs.PA-CF: Highest stiffness and heat resistance (snippet: HDT 215 C at 0.45 MPa for PA6-CF20) and the best chemical resistance, but PA6 swells with humidity, which works against dimensional accuracy; PA12-CF absorbs less.

note: PETG in black is the pragmatic choice; print the 28 C enclosure spare parts in the same material. Keep liquid resin off any of these plastics rather than relying on resistance.
